title: How Long Does Concrete Sealer Last in Ontario
metaTitle: How Long Does Concrete Sealer Last in Ontario
metaDescription: Ontario winters test concrete sealer harder than most climates. Here is what actually determines how long a coat holds up and when to plan resealing.
excerpt: Freeze-thaw cycles and road salt make Southwestern Ontario one of the tougher climates for a concrete sealer to hold up in. Here is what actually shortens or extends that lifespan.
heroAlt: Sealed concrete driveway in Woodstock Ontario showing an even wet-look sheen after fresh sealer application
keyTakeaways: A quality sealer typically protects concrete for 2 to 5 years in Southwestern Ontario, with the range depending far more on traffic and exposure than on the product itself.
Freeze-thaw cycling, road salt from Highway 401 corridor winters, and direct sun exposure are the three factors that shorten sealer life fastest in this region.
Driveways and areas that see vehicle traffic and winter salt wear out sooner than patios, walkways, or shaded areas.
The clearest sign it is time to reseal is water no longer beading on the surface, not a specific date on a calendar.
All-Seal offers a free on-site inspection to assess your existing sealer and give you a realistic timeline rather than a generic estimate.

body.text: One of the most common questions homeowners ask before booking a sealing job is simple: how long is this actually going to last. It is a fair question, and the honest answer is that it depends on where the concrete sits, what it is used for, and how many winters it has to survive. In Southwestern Ontario, that answer skews toward the shorter end of the range compared to milder climates, because this region combines two of the harshest conditions a sealer can face: repeated freeze-thaw cycling and heavy winter road salt. Understanding what actually wears sealer down helps you plan realistically instead of guessing.
The general range: 2 to 5 years

A properly applied acrylic, polyurethane, or penetrating sealer generally holds up for somewhere between 2 and 5 years before it needs a fresh coat. That is a wide range, and the reason it is wide is that traffic and exposure matter more than the sealer itself. A driveway that sees daily vehicle traffic, winter plowing, and de-icing salt is going to wear on the shorter end of that window. A shaded patio that only sees foot traffic in warmer months can stretch well past the midpoint. All-Seal's own track record across driveways, patios and other surfaces in Oxford County and the surrounding area reflects that same pattern: the surfaces exposed to the most abuse are the ones that need attention soonest.
Why Ontario winters are hard on sealer specifically

Freeze-thaw cycling is the biggest factor unique to this climate. Southwestern Ontario does not get one long, steady winter freeze. It gets repeated swings above and below zero, sometimes within the same week, as moisture in the concrete's pores freezes, expands, and thaws again. A good sealer is doing real work here: blocking water from getting into the concrete in the first place, which is what prevents that freeze-thaw expansion from cracking and scaling the surface underneath. As the sealer itself ages and thins from UV exposure and abrasion, its ability to block that water intake gradually declines, which is part of why resealing on a predictable schedule matters more here than in a climate that never sees ice.
Road salt and the Highway 401 corridor effect

The second major factor is salt. Communities along and near the Highway 401 corridor, including Woodstock, Brantford, and Cambridge, see heavy de-icing salt use on both public roads and private driveways through the winter months. Salt is corrosive to unprotected concrete and accelerates surface scaling, and it also breaks down sealer coatings faster than plain water exposure would. A driveway that gets salted every winter, or that tracks salt in from a garage floor, is going to see its sealer degrade noticeably faster than a patio that never touches a de-icer. This is one of the main reasons driveways and garage floors tend to sit at the 2 to 3 year end of the lifespan range, while patios and walkways that avoid salt exposure often make it closer to 4 or 5 years.
Sun, humidity, and the rest of the year

Winter is not the only season working against a sealer coat. Southwestern Ontario summers bring plenty of direct sun and humidity, and UV exposure is a steady, cumulative stress on any sealer, particularly a high-gloss acrylic finish sitting on a south-facing driveway or an unshaded pool deck. Humidity does not damage sealer the way freeze-thaw or salt does, but it does mean concrete stays damp longer after rain, which matters if a sealer coat has already thinned and is no longer shedding water effectively. Surfaces with full sun exposure and no shade cover tend to show UV-related dulling before they show any structural wear, which is often the first visible sign that a recoat is coming.
Traffic and use matter as much as climate

items: Driveways with daily vehicle traffic and winter salt: typically 2 to 3 years
Garage floors with hot tire pickup and de-icing salt tracked in: typically 2 to 3 years
Pool decks with chlorine exposure and full sun: typically 3 years
Patios and walkways with foot traffic only, less salt exposure: typically 3 to 4 years
Shaded or low-traffic surfaces: often 4 to 5 years

body.text: These ranges are starting points, not guarantees, because two driveways in the same neighbourhood can wear differently depending on how much they are used, whether snow gets shovelled or scraped aggressively, and what kind of de-icing product gets used. A property that relies on sand instead of salt, for instance, tends to be gentler on sealer than one using rock salt or calcium chloride regularly.
The real sign it is time to reseal

Rather than marking a date on the calendar, the most reliable indicator that a sealer has reached the end of its useful life is a simple water test. Pour a small amount of water on the concrete: if it beads up and sits on the surface, the sealer is still doing its job. If the water soaks in and darkens the concrete instead of beading, the sealer has thinned past the point of protecting against water infiltration, salt penetration, and freeze-thaw damage, and it is time to plan a recoat. Other visible signs include a surface that looks dull or chalky compared to when it was first sealed, faded colour on stained or decorative concrete, and the reappearance of small surface stains from oil or dirt that a fresh sealer coat would normally repel.

The water-bead test takes thirty seconds and tells you more than any calendar estimate. If water soaks in instead of beading, book a free inspection before the next freeze-thaw cycle takes advantage of it.
What happens if you wait too long

Letting a sealer fail completely before resealing is the most expensive way to handle this. Once the coating is gone, the concrete underneath is exposed to everything it was protected from: water infiltration that drives freeze-thaw scaling and spalling, salt that corrodes the surface, oil stains from a garage floor or driveway, and UV fading on any decorative or stamped finish. At that point, sealing does not just restore protection, it often requires more prep work, such as addressing surface damage or repairing cracks and joints, before a new coat can go down properly. Catching the surface while the old sealer is fading but the concrete underneath is still sound keeps the job simpler and the concrete in better shape long term.
Sealing over an existing coat

The good news is that resealing does not usually mean starting from scratch. All-Seal works on previously sealed surfaces regularly, assessing the condition of the existing coating and stripping it only where it is failing or incompatible with the new product. A typical resealing job still starts with a full pressure wash and cleaning, addresses any crack or joint repair needed after a few winters of freeze-thaw stress, and then applies a fresh coat once the surface is completely dry. For a closer look at that process, see our guide on /resources/can-you-seal-over-previously-sealed-concrete.
Choosing a sealer with your timeline in mind

If you know a surface is going to see heavy winter salt and daily traffic, that is worth factoring into the sealer choice up front. Acrylic sealers offer strong protection and a range of sheen options from /finishes, including High Gloss, Semi-Gloss, and Matte, and hold up well on most driveways and patios. Polyurethane sealers tend to offer stronger durability under heavier wear, which is worth discussing for a driveway or garage floor that takes a real beating every winter. Penetrating sealers work differently, soaking into the concrete rather than forming a surface film, and can be the right call in specific situations depending on the concrete's age and porosity. An anti-slip additive is also worth considering for steps, pool decks, or any area from /services/pool-deck-sealing where wet footing is a concern, regardless of which sheen you choose.
Planning around Ontario's sealing season

Resealing works best when it happens in warmer, drier stretches of the year, giving the concrete time to fully dry before the sealer goes on and time to cure before winter arrives. Homeowners in Woodstock, St. Thomas, Brantford, Hamilton, Kitchener-Waterloo, and Cambridge who know their sealer is nearing the end of its life are better off booking a free inspection in late summer or early fall rather than waiting until the first frost puts pressure on the schedule. faq.q: How long does concrete sealer last in Ontario compared to warmer climates?
faq.a: Ontario's freeze-thaw cycling and heavy winter road salt tend to wear sealer down faster than in climates without hard winters, which is why the typical range here runs 2 to 5 years rather than longer.

faq.q: Does a driveway need resealing more often than a patio?
faq.a: Usually yes. Driveways see vehicle traffic and winter salt exposure that patios generally avoid, which is why driveways often need resealing every 2 to 3 years while patios can stretch to 4 or 5.

faq.q: How do I know if my sealer has worn off?
faq.a: Pour water on the surface. If it beads up, the sealer is still working. If it soaks in and darkens the concrete, the sealer has thinned and it is time to plan a recoat.

faq.q: Can salt actually damage sealed concrete?
faq.a: Yes. Road salt and de-icing products break down sealer coatings faster than plain water exposure, and once the sealer is gone, salt can corrode the unprotected concrete surface underneath.

faq.q: Do I need to strip old sealer before resealing?
faq.a: Not always. All-Seal assesses the existing coating during the free inspection and strips it only where it is failing or incompatible with the new sealer, which keeps most resealing jobs simpler than a full strip-and-start-over.

faq.q: What is the best time of year to reseal in Southwestern Ontario?
faq.a: Late summer or early fall works well, since it gives the concrete time to dry completely and the new sealer time to cure before winter freeze-thaw cycles begin.
